findings.finding: The one-hop rule (Approach step 3) trusts whatever commit refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch> points to, and the plan never checks that this commit is not the change under review. In this repo's unchanged CI workflow, push events fetch the pushed branch into refs/remotes/origin/<branch>, and the hop target is fetched only in that case. So when main's committed [snapshot].ref names origin/<branch> and someone pushes to <branch>, the gate takes its trust configuration (trusted_opcert_keys, require_environment, tracker.dir) from the pushed commit itself. That brings back the self-configuration hole (golden-busied-nag) this module exists to close. The branch's write access may also be looser than main's branch protection, and the plan does not say so.

Take a base resolved through refs/remotes/origin/HEAD -> origin/main, with a committed `ref = "origin/main"` (the common value). Compared by name, the two differ and the gate makes a pointless hop. That hop could also exit 2 in some fetch shapes. Second, it does not say how '<remote>/<branch>' is split when the branch (e.g. 'release/1.x') or the remote name contains '/'.
findings.location: Approach step 3 (One reviewed hop)
scenarios: origin/HEAD -> origin/main, and the committed [snapshot].ref is "origin/main". A name comparison sees a difference and hops to the same branch.
Committed ref "origin/release/1.x". Splitting at the first '/' gives remote 'origin' and branch 'release/1.x'. Matching against the configured remote names is the safer rule but is not stated.
findings.suggested_fix: Resolve the base with `git rev-parse --symbolic-full-name` and skip the hop when the hop target names the same full ref. Parse the committed value by matching the longest configured remote name followed by '/', and treat the rest as the branch.

elgui/charter issue #26 describes the same pattern: a fallback that trusts origin/HEAD before origin/main lets a stale origin/HEAD in a long-lived clone narrow what gets gated.
findings.finding: The plan frames a stale `<remote>/HEAD` only as a usability limit ('fixed with `git remote set-head`'). Prior art for this exact ordering (trusting origin/HEAD before origin/main) treats it as a trust hazard. In this gate, the base decides which committed `[verify] trusted_opcert_keys` / `require_environment` apply. A clone whose `<remote>/HEAD` still names the old default branch would gate against that branch's rebar.toml. That file may carry keys revoked since, or a laxer policy, and the old branch may no longer be protected after the switch. The plan does not weigh this against the threat model it states ('the base ref decides which `rebar.toml` the gate trusts').
findings.location: Approach step 2 (branch resolution order and the 'known limit' sentence)
scenarios: An upstream switches its default branch from `master` to `main` and leaves `master` in place, unprotected. A long-lived verifier clone still has origin/HEAD→origin/master, so verify-opcert reads master's rebar.toml. That file may still trust a key the project has since removed, or someone with push access to the now-unprotected master can change it.

findings.finding: The one-hop rule accepts a committed `[snapshot].ref` of the form `<remote>/<branch>` naming ANY configured remote, not the remote the base was resolved from. Remote names are local conventions. A committed `origin/release` written for canonical clones means, in a fork-workflow checkout where `REBAR_SYNC_REMOTE=upstream` and `origin` is the developer's fork, the fork's `release` branch. The author of the change controls that branch. The gate would then trust a rebar.toml that did not come from the reviewed base, contradicting the plan's stated constraint.
findings.location: Approach step 3 ('if it sets `[snapshot].ref` to a `<remote>/<branch>` form naming a configured remote ... re-resolves to `refs/remotes/<remote>/<branch>`')
scenarios: Fork workflow: REBAR_SYNC_REMOTE=upstream, and upstream/main's committed ref is `origin/release`. The hop goes to origin/release on the contributor's fork, and the gate reads a config the contributor can edit.
Same setup with a remote whose name is not configured locally: the hop is silently ignored and the gate reads main's config without telling the user that the configured base was not followed.
findings.suggested_fix: Change step 3 to: follow `<remote>/<branch>` only when `<remote>` equals the step-1 remote. If it names a different remote, ignore it with a printed notice (or raise ConfigError), and say which in the help.

tests/unit/test_opcert_gate_config.py:62 `init --bare -b main` and :74 `_git(repo, "fetch", "-q", "origin")`, a default-refspec fetch.
Git 2.48 release notes: fetch now sets refs/remotes/$remote/HEAD when it is missing, and honours remote.<remote>.followRemoteHEAD.
GitHub blog (Git 2.48 highlights): setting followRemoteHead to warn or always makes fetch warn about, or automatically update, a stale origin/HEAD.
phantompane/phantom PR #861 shows prior art for the test hazard: its 'no remote HEAD' fixtures had to set followRemoteHEAD=never to stay headless on every Git version.
findings.finding: The plan's account of how `<remote>/HEAD` gets recorded predates Git 2.48. Since 2.48, a default-refspec `git fetch` creates refs/remotes/<remote>/HEAD when it is missing, and the `remote.<name>.followRemoteHEAD` setting (warn/always) can keep it current. This affects the plan in two ways. (a) The 'stale `<remote>/HEAD` after a rename' known limit has an existing git-native remedy (`git config remote.<remote>.followRemoteHEAD always`) that the error text and help should mention. That is a git setting, not a rebar key, so it does not breach the no-new-key rule. (b) The existing fixture `_repo_with_origin` runs a plain `git fetch -q origin` against a bare repo with HEAD→main, so whether origin/HEAD exists after setup depends on the installed git version. New tests for 'dangling origin/HEAD falls through', 'no resolvable base' and 'master with origin/HEAD' must set or delete the symref explicitly, or pin followRemoteHEAD=never, or they will test different code paths on different machines.
findings.location: Approach step 2 ('A stale `<remote>/HEAD` … is a known limit'); Testing section; tests/unit/test_opcert_gate_config.py:59-75 (_repo_with_origin)
scenarios: A developer on git ≥ 2.48 runs the new 'no origin/HEAD → origin/main' test. The fixture's fetch already created origin/HEAD, so the fallthrough branch is never exercised. CI on older git takes a different path.
A user hits the stale-HEAD limit. The help suggests a one-off set-head and does not mention the persistent followRemoteHEAD=always setting git offers for exactly this case.
findings.suggested_fix: In the Testing section, state that fixtures control `<remote>/HEAD` explicitly: call `git remote set-head origin -d` (or fetch with `-c remote.origin.followRemoteHEAD=never`) for the absent and dangling cases, and `git remote set-head origin master` for the master case. In the error/help text for stale-HEAD, add: 'or run `git config remote.<remote>.followRemoteHEAD always` (git ≥ 2.48) so fetches keep it current'.
